newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks seen hovering, awaiting output data.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks seen hovering, awaiting output data.

text.p: Tokyo stocks are expected to hover in the Friday session as investors wait for industrial output data and forecasts to be released in the afternoon for more clues on the health of the economy, brokers said.
On Thursday, The 225-share Nikkei average closed down 54.51 points, or 0.26 percent, at 20,624.76.
The index hit a new 1997 intra-day high of 20,910.79 soon after the opening but it fell short of the key 21,000 threshold. Its September futures finished 60 points lower at 20,700.

"The market had been encouraged by the better-than-expected Bank of Japan 'tankan', but many investors are still a bit sceptical about the recovery of the economy," said Yasuo Ueki, general manager at Nikko Securities.
"If the industrial output data is also bullish, investors will gain more confidence, but if the figures are bearish, there may be some disappointment," he said.
Brokers said, however, that the downside was considered limited as investment trusts were due to be launched during the day. They said the recent growth in turnover was also encouraging.

"Rather than new purchases, much of the buying seen today in banks and brokerages is part of short-covering moves following a huge sell-off in January," said Seiki Orimi, an analyst at Dai-Ichi Securities.
"The market is still waiting to see what sort of punitive measures will be taken against Nomura following the scandal."
Turnover was a modest 193 million shares compared to the 310 million traded by midday on Thursday.
Losers outstripped winners 679 to 352, while 210 issues were unchanged, but trade was basically directionless, brokers said.

"There was some buying interest in the morning, but the Nikkei average ended Thursday lamely and the yen is stalled at 113 to the dollar making investors cautious," a trader at a second-tier brokerage said.
The Nikkei hit a new high for calendar 1997 on Thursday morning, but ended in negative territory.

Brokers said market participants were hoping that industrial output figures for May and forecasts for June and July due out at 0430 GMT would provide some sort of clue on which way the Nikkei average was going.
By sector, air transportation, credit/lease, pulp/paper and construction topped the list of gainers.
Railway/bus, retailing, real estate, banks and rubber headed the list of retreaters.
The TOPIX shed 13.10 points, or 0.84 percent, to end the two-hour morning session at 1,547.18. The Nikkei 300 fell 2.50 points, or 0.83 percent, to 300.04.
